title: Was Napoleon Really Short? A Number Read With the Wrong Ruler
description:
In May 1821, on the South Atlantic island of Saint Helena, a doctor wrote Napoleon's height into the autopsy report: 5 feet 2 inches. The number wasn't wrong. But read with a French ruler or an English one, the same number differs by more than 10 centimeters.

This episode follows that number: what the old French foot and inch come to in centimeters, how tall French men were on average at the time, the "Little Boney" of the English cartoonist Gillray, the minimum height for the Imperial Guard grenadiers, the "little" in the nickname "the Little Corporal", and the "Napoleon complex", a name that only appeared a hundred years later.

The source of every number, year and work is listed in the references below; conversions are based on the old French measure (pied du roi) and English lengths. We found no source that says outright whether the autopsy used the old foot or the "everyday" foot introduced in 1812 (one third of a meter); the valet's 5 feet 2 inches 3 lines and the English craftsman's 5 feet 7 inches both match the old-measure reading. Sentences that begin "We think" are this channel's view.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. Historical figures are drawn as cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant to resemble anyone; modern researchers are not drawn.

Information as of 2026-10-19

chapters.island: 1821: 5 feet 2 inches, written on Saint Helena
chapters.antommarchi: With a French ruler, he was taller than the average Frenchman
chapters.first-clue: A 26-year-old general the veterans called "the Little Corporal"
chapters.print-shop: "Little Boney" in English cartoons, nearly 20 years before the autopsy
chapters.borrowed-name: "Napoleon complex": a name born a century after his death

np101.text: May 1821. The South Atlantic. A small island called Saint Helena.

np102.text: In his house on the island, a doctor measures him with a ruler.

np103.text: The man who just died in there was once Europe's most famous man.

np104.text: The height he wrote down: 5 feet 2 inches.

np106.text: But many later remembered another, even shorter Napoleon.

np108.text: While he was alive, a British cartoonist already drew him as a little man stamping in a childish rage.

np109.text: Around him, there often stood unusually tall soldiers.

np110.text: Over a century later, his name was borrowed to label a kind of temper.

np111.text: So how tall was Napoleon, really?

np201.text: The doctor who wrote the report was Napoleon's own physician, and he used a French ruler.

np202.text: The report goes further: 5 feet 2 inches plus 4 lines.

np217.text: An inch was split into twelve lines, so four lines is a third of an inch.

np203.text: By then, France already had the meter.

np204.text: An old French foot was about 32.5 centimeters; an English foot, just 30.5.

np205.text: Same with the inch: the French one was a bit longer.

np206.text: So what if you read the same number with an English ruler?

np207.text: In old French units, that's about 168 or 169 centimeters.

np208.text: Read in English units, it's only 157 centimeters.

np218.text: The two readings differ by 11 centimeters.

np224.text: There's actually a third reading: by the everyday foot used from 1812, he'd be 4 centimeters taller still.

np223.text: If the doctor had written meters, we wouldn't have to guess which foot he meant.

np209.text: Was that short for the time?

np210.text: Scholars reckon adult French men then averaged about 164 or 165 centimeters.

np222.text: It's based on Napoleon-era conscription: the heights measured on recruits around twenty.

np211.text: He was a few centimeters above that average.

np221.text: Next to today's average Taiwanese man, he really isn't tall.

np212.text: His valet's memoir gives 5 feet 2 inches 3 lines, just one line off the doctor's.

np219.text: The English craftsman who handled his funeral used an English ruler: 5 feet 7 inches.

np213.text: So where did "short Napoleon" come from?

np418.text: When he was still young, his veterans gave him a nickname.

np407.text: That was 1796. He was 26, leading an army in Italy.

np420.text: He had to take a wooden bridge at Lodi, nearly 200 meters long, with Austrian cannons on the far bank.

np408.text: His troops charged across under fire.

np417.text: Las Cases, who joined him there, wrote: after each battle, veterans met to "promote" the young general a rank.

np409.text: After Lodi, they "made" him corporal, and "the Little Corporal" spread through the ranks.

np411.text: In French, "little" can also be affectionate, like calling a buddy "little Joe."

np412.text: Corporal is a very low rank; the usual view is that the veterans were claiming the general as one of their own.

np419.text: But those who drew him short were mostly across the Channel.

np301.text: In 1803, he often hung in London print-shop windows.

np302.text: That May, Britain and France went to war again.

np303.text: A popular London cartoonist, Gillray, made nearly 1,000 satirical prints in his lifetime.

np320.text: No. He never once saw Napoleon in person.

np304.text: Remember that little man stamping his feet?

np305.text: Gillray drew Napoleon as a tiny man, stamping, shaking his fists and yelling.

np328.text: He's often far shorter than those around him, with an oversized hat.

np401.text: The next year he became emperor. Remember those very tall soldiers?

np402.text: They were his Imperial Guard: the grenadiers.

np403.text: Guard grenadiers had a minimum height, well above the typical man.

np404.text: Add tall bearskin hats, and they stood beside the emperor.

np405.text: An average-height man in a row of tall ones looks a size smaller.

np415.text: He often wore a plain gray coat and an unplumed hat; among gold-braided officers, that made him easiest to spot.

np307.text: Another, from 1805: he and the British prime minister carve a globe-shaped pudding.

np308.text: The PM is tall and thin; he's short and stout.

np317.text: Wilder yet: Britain's king holds him in his palm, eyes him through a spyglass, calls him a vile little reptile.

np309.text: Passersby crowded at the shop window to look.

np310.text: Through a decade-plus of war, British cartoons kept it up.

np327.text: Other prints called him "the little Corsican."

np325.text: Did he care what Britain wrote?

np318.text: He did. France formally asked Britain to rein in the papers that attacked him.

np311.text: In 1815, Napoleon lost at Waterloo; Gillray died that same year.

np321.text: That summer, the beaten Napoleon was held on a British warship off the harbor.

np323.text: Over a thousand boats, thousands of Britons, rowed out just to see him.

np322.text: Its British captain later wrote: he was sturdy, about 5 feet 7 inches tall.

np312.text: But that stamping little man stuck around.

np319.text: After Gillray, another cartoonist, Cruikshank, kept drawing him small.

np314.text: Remember the 157 from reading it with an English ruler?

np315.text: Read that way, the number fits the little man in the cartoons perfectly.

np530.text: That's how, in English, he became a small man.

np528.text: Remember that temper from the start? The earliest known use of the name is in a 1923 American newspaper.

np531.text: Back then it meant self-importance, not height.

np502.text: People later tied it to Viennese psychologist Adler's theory.

np503.text: Adler said people try to make up for what they feel inferior in.

np504.text: Only later was it pinned on short men: short, so extra competitive and combative.

np521.text: Today, it's in the American Merriam-Webster dictionary.

np506.text: Napoleon himself never heard the term.

np526.text: When he died, Adler hadn't even been born.

np509.text: So are short men really more aggressive?

np533.text: A British experiment in 2007 said: no.

np529.text: A 2018 Dutch study found short men weren't more aggressive, but when splitting things themselves, they kept a bit more.

np527.text: Whatever the studies say, the term is a century old.

np510.text: We think the name caught on so easily thanks to over a century of cartoons before it.

np532.text: The 5 feet 2 inches he wrote down was never short at all.

np513.text: Where'd you first hear he was short?

np514.text: We only cover what the records show. Subscribe to open the files with us.
